newsitem.title: USA: U.S. utility SO2 emissions beat federal standards.
newsitem.headline: U.S. utility SO2 emissions beat federal standards.

text.p: U.S. power plants trimmed their sulfur dioxide emissions in 1996 35 percent more than required and cut nitrogen oxide emissions 18 percent more than required, the Environmental Protection Agency said Friday.
Sulfur dioxide emissions in 1996 were 2.9 million tons below the 8.3 million ton allowable level under the agency's Clean Air Act acid rain program.
At the same time, utilities subject to the first phase of nitrogen oxide (NOx) regulations had cut their emission rates on average by 40 percent below 1990 levels.
"The results are impressive for the first year of compliance with Phase I NOx regulations," the EPA said in the 1996 report on its acid rain program under the Clean Air Act.
Under the EPA's sulfur dioxide emissions trading prgram, 4.4 million trades were reported in 1996, more than double the level in the previous year.
The average price of a sulfur dioxide allowance fell to $68 in 1996 from $130 in 1995, "partially in response to the low costs of compliance encountered in 1995," EPA said.
"Also a factor in the low allowance price was the vast overcompliance and the resulting substantial bank of allowances," EPA said.

Because of their success in curbing emissions cheaply, power plants are expected to be a major target for further smog-fighting efforts in the eastern half of the United States within the next few years, under an agreement reached Thursday by the 37-state Ozone Transport Assessment Group.
